issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration together with consequential relief is not barred from being heard merely because the plaintiff fails to prove the consequential relief.
material_facts: The suit sought a declaration of ownership and an injunction against interference with the property.
The plaintiff failed to prove possession, so the injunction could not be granted.
The trial court found that the plaintiff had proved ownership.
issues.conclusion: The suit could not be dismissed as not maintainable under the proviso to Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, because the plaint sought consequential relief as well as a declaration; failure on the consequential relief was a matter of merits, not maintainability.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the proviso bars a declaration where a plaintiff able to seek further relief seeks only a declaration and omits that relief. Whether the proviso applies is assessed from the plaint as framed. Where consequential relief is claimed, failure to prove that relief does not make the suit unmaintainable. The Court relied on M. K. Rappai v. John, Ram Saran v. Smt. Ganga Devi, Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra, and Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy, and rejected the contrary approach in Sri Aralappa v. Sri Jagannath.

predicates.declaratory_suit_with_consequential_clai: The plaintiff filed a suit seeking a declaration of a right together with relief intended to give effect to that right.
predicates.consequential_relief_unproved: The plaintiff failed to establish the facts necessary to obtain the consequential relief sought.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeks both a declaration and consequential relief, failure to prove the consequential relief does not, by itself, make the suit unmaintainable for omission of further relief.

issues.legal_issue: A proven ownership claim may support a declaration of ownership even when the plaintiff has failed to prove possession and cannot obtain consequential relief.
material_facts: The trial court found that the plaintiff had proved ownership of the property, and that finding was not displaced on appeal.
The plaintiff failed to prove possession and therefore could not obtain an injunction against interference.
The request to add a claim for possession at the appellate stage was rejected.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to a declaration of ownership notwithstanding the failure to establish possession or obtain consequential relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 does not prohibit a standalone declaratory decree where the proviso does not apply. A declaration may be granted on a proven right even if it is non-executable or the plaintiff fails on consequential relief. The Court relied on the principles in M. K. Rappai v. John, Ram Saran v. Smt. Ganga Devi, Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra, and Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy, and held that Sri Aralappa v. Sri Jagannath was not good law insofar as it required dismissal of the declaration claim in these circumstances.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking a declaration of a right to property.
predicates.ownership_established: The fact-finding court found that the claimant had proved ownership, and that finding was not displaced on appeal.
predicates.consequential_relief_unproved: The claimant failed to establish the facts necessary to obtain the consequential relief sought.

issues.definition: In a declaratory suit, when ownership is established, failure to prove consequential relief does not prevent a declaration of ownership.

issues.legal_issue: An injunction against interference with property cannot be granted when the claimant has not established possession.
material_facts: The earlier suit for an injunction had been dismissed because the plaintiff failed to establish possession.
In the later suit, the plaintiff did not demonstrate that possession had been recovered after the earlier suit.
The plaintiff had admitted that the opposing party was in possession and cultivating the property.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not entitled to the injunction sought because they had not established possession of the property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that injunctive relief against interference with property could not be granted without proof that the plaintiff was in possession. It distinguished Devish v. M. K. Subbiah and Navalram Laxmidas Devmurari v. Vijayaben Jayvantbhai Chavda, where the fact-finding courts had affirmatively found possession, and found that the presumption that possession follows title did not assist the plaintiff in light of the evidence of the opposing party’s possession.

predicates.property_injunction_claim: The claimant sought an injunction restraining another person from interfering with the claimant's possession of property.
predicates.claimant_possession_not_established: The claimant did not prove possession of the property, and the evidence showed that another person was in possession.

issues.definition: A claimant seeking an injunction against interference with property is denied that relief when the claimant has not established possession.

issues.legal_issue: A later suit based on alleged interference occurring after an earlier injunction suit is not barred merely because the later suit includes a claim for declaration that could not have been made in the earlier suit.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought an injunction and was dismissed because the plaintiff failed to establish possession.
The later suit relied on alleged interference occurring after the earlier suit and sought a declaration and an injunction.
The later claim for declaration arose from the subsequent alleged incidents.
issues.conclusion: Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 did not bar the later suit on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 did not apply because the later claim for declaration was based on subsequent alleged incidents of interference and could not have been included in the earlier suit. The claim could fail on its merits, but the suit could not be dismissed on that ground under Order II Rule 2.

predicates.successive_suits: The claimant brought a later suit after an earlier suit concerning the same property or dispute.
predicates.later_claim_based_on_subsequent_events: The later suit relied on alleged events that occurred after the earlier suit was brought.
predicates.later_claim_unavailable_in_earlier_suit: The claim in the later suit could not have been included in the earlier suit when it was brought.

issues.definition: A later suit is not barred for omission of a claim from the earlier suit when the later claim is based on subsequent events and was unavailable in the earlier suit.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment adding a claim for possession may be refused when it is sought after the applicable limitation period has expired.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought, at the appellate stage, to amend the plaint to add an alternative claim for possession.
The plaintiffs had been aware from the earlier proceedings that they were not found to be in possession.
The High Court found the explanation for the delay unsatisfactory, and the amendment was found to be outside the prescribed limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The rejection of the amendment seeking possession was upheld because the amendment was not sought within the applicable limitation period.
issues.legal_principle: A plaintiff may seek to amend a plaint to add an omitted relief, but the amendment must be saved by limitation. The Court relied on Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra and Venkataraja v. Vidyane Doureradjaperumal; it also referred to Parkash Chand Khurana v. Harnam Singh and State of M.P. v. Mangilal Sharma for the requirement that defendants raise the issue at the earliest.

predicates.appellate_amendment_request: A party asked an appellate court to amend the pleadings in an existing suit.
predicates.added_possession_claim: The requested amendment would add a claim to recover possession of property.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The time allowed for bringing the added claim had expired before the amendment was sought.

issues.definition: An appellate request to add a claim for possession is refused when the limitation period for that claim has expired.
